place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 柴房后面 · 泥地里
place.en: Chending Temple · Behind the woodshed · in the mud

setup.zh: 胸口的木牌烫了，烫得很久很久。小银狐钻出来，看着你的伤，一句话都没说——然后「呸」地吐出了一样东西。
setup.en: The token on your chest burns, and burns a long while. The little silver fox slips out, looks at your hurts and says nothing at all — then spits something out.

recap.zh: 银月一句话都没说，吐出了她肚里的一只巴掌大的小铜家伙。「替本王看着它。」她说完最后半句就淡了下去：「……下次……打回去……」
recap.en: Yinyue said nothing at all; she spat out something from her belly — a little bronze thing the size of a palm. "Look after it for me." Her last half-sentence as she faded: "…next time… hit back…"

zh: 一只巴掌大的小铜家伙，圆肚子，三只脚，两只耳。
en: A bronze thing the size of a palm: round belly, three legs, two ears.
"From my belly. Swallowed it who knows what year…"
"…What's your name?" The lid does not stir.

label.en: The little beast on the lid

text.zh: 小兽闭着眼，只在你肚子咕咕叫的时候，才睁一睁。
text.en: The little beast keeps its eyes shut — it opens them only when your stomach growls.

text.zh: 山，水，一条弯弯的河，河边一座方方的城。你一拃拃不满它半圈。
text.en: Mountains, water, a winding river, and by it a square-walled town. Your hand's span won't reach halfway round.

text.zh: 圆滚滚的，一层绿锈，锈底下透着一点暗金，摸上去温温的，倒像刚吃饱了什么。
text.en: Round as a pot, green with rust, a dull gold under the rust; warm to the touch, as if it had just eaten its fill.

story.zh:
胸口的木牌，便在这时烫了起来。

这一回烫得很久很久，久到小狰都觉出不对来，从他胸口上爬下去，蹲在一旁看。银月从木牌里慢慢地钻了出来。它比那一夜又薄了些，月光从它身上透过去，他能看见它身后的月亮。它低下头来，看着他肿成馒头的那只眼睛，一直看到月亮从它身后挪过去一指。

它平日嘴那么毒，说他吵，说他傻，说他是漏勺。这时候，它却一句话也没有说。然后它张开嘴，「呸」的一声，吐出一样东西来，落在他胸口上，「叮」的一声——不像铜，倒像极远的山寺里敲了一记钟，在他胸腔里嗡了好一会儿。

那是一只巴掌大的小铜家伙，圆滚滚一个肚子，底下三只脚，口沿上竖着两只耳朵，周身一层绿锈，锈底下透着一点暗金，倒像村里祠堂供桌上那口香炉，给人捏小了一百倍。口上扣着一个盖，盖上蹲着一只小兽，打了个哈欠，睁开一只眼睛瞥了他一眼，又闭上了。银月道：「本王肚里的。不知哪年吞的，吃了本王好些年的灵气。替本王看着它。它什么都吃；喂它，它吐东西；吐什么，看你的命——十回里九回，是破烂。喂凡物，多半出凡物；想出仙品，得喂仙品。开一回，吃你一口。」小满叫道：「银月？」

「下次，」她道，「打回去。」

话音一落，她便像灶膛里一缕烟丝，不见了。

小满一把将木牌攥在手心里，叫了两声「银月」，没有应。那只蜷着的小狐狸还在，九条尾巴里原先亮着的那一条，这时候是暗的。他盯着它看，盯到手心里全是汗，才看见那条尾巴极慢极慢地，亮了一下，又暗了下去。

还在。

他这才出了一口长气，出得太猛，肋骨疼得他弯下腰去。下次，打回去。她不是叫他今天还手。她是说，今天，就这样；下次，打回去。他把这五个字，在心里放好了。

今夜，就是马小宝说的那半个月的头一夜。

他扶着柴垛站起来，肋骨那儿「咯」的一声，又跪了下去。断了，至少一根。他从柴堆最底下摸出巡夜令，挂回腰上，把小狰和那只小铜炉一并揣进怀里。墙是翻不过去了，墙根底下有个排水的豁口，他趴下去，一点一点地爬出去，爬上后山的小路。一丈路，他歇三回；歇的时候，不敢喘深，只照着那个不深不浅的口子，一口，一口。月亮从这一头挪到那一头，他才爬到药园门口，掀开挂在园门边的巡夜簿，手上不知是泥是血，往十二夜那一格上一按，便是一个黑红的手印子。

他就这么背靠着园门，坐到了天亮。

天快亮的时候，小路上有脚步声，一步一停。是孙二狗，手里攥着一块井水浸过的布。孙二狗的铺挨着通铺那扇小窗，柴房后面那块空地，从那扇窗看出去，看得一清二楚。他蹲下，把那块布按在小满肿起来的左眼上，半天，才小声道：「……我没出来。」小满道：「我知道。」孙二狗道：「我怕。」小满道：「我也怕。怕，又不丢人。」孙二狗低着头，两只耳朵慢慢地红了，道：「等我……站得稳了。」后半句，他没说出来。

十月十三，小满让孙二狗架着，去了饭堂。他想，不去，就更像有事了。满饭堂的人偷偷地看他，看完了又偷偷地看马小宝。谁都知道是怎么回事。谁也没有说。马小宝端着空碗从他桌边经过，拿指头在他肩膀上戳了一戳，正戳在第二十三下那个地方：「师弟，摔得不轻啊。好好躺着，药园那头，有师兄呢。」

阿禾从山上下来了——她卯时进药园，在巡夜簿上看见了十二夜那一格。她端着碗在他对面坐下，先看他的脸，从左眼看到嘴角，道：「谁？」小满道：「摔的。」阿禾在本子上记了一笔，拿手挡着，他还是瞥见了一个圈。阿禾道：「你衣裳上的泥印子。一个印子一下。我数的。二十三。」小满吃了一惊。她从碗底下摸出一个煮鸡蛋，还是温的，放在他面前：「吃了。」小满道：「……记账？」阿禾拿起炭条，落到纸上，停了很久，炭条的尖儿在纸上压出一个小黑点，慢慢洇开了一圈。后来她记了一笔，合上本子，道：「利息，这回……先不算。」端起碗走了，一次也没回头。

出了饭堂，药房门口停着济世堂送药材的挑子，挑子后头跟着一个光着两只脚的跑腿孩子。小满认出来了：廊下喊「那我就当那一个」的，就是他。那孩子从怀里掏出一封信来，信封上是舅舅的字：外甥沈小满亲启。

信不长。家里都好，勿念。娘的眼睛，夜里做针线熬坏了一点，不打紧。埋石蛋那夜，是这孩子帮我挖的坑。末了一行，字写得小了：**你爹如今天天进黑松岭。马家的狗不过断碑，他过。膝盖比去年重了，阴天下不了炕，晴天照去。我劝不住。**

小满把那封信看了三遍，揣进了怀里，贴着木牌。

那天辰时，小满没去讲堂。他蹲在柴房里，面前摆着那只小铜炉，跟它说话：「你叫什么？」炉盖一动不动。
story.en:
Just then the token on his chest grew hot.

This time the heat lasted a long, long while, so long that even Little Zheng sensed something wrong, climbed down off his chest and sat to one side, watching. Slowly, Silver Moon came out of the token. It was thinner again than that night; moonlight went through it, and he could see the moon behind it. It bent its head and looked at his eye, swollen up like a steamed bun, and kept looking until the moon behind it had moved a finger's width.

For all its usual poison — he was noisy, he was stupid, he was a skimmer — at this moment it said nothing at all. Then it opened its mouth, *ptoo*, and spat something out; it landed on his chest with a *ting* — not like bronze, more like a bell struck in some far mountain temple, humming in his chest a long while.

It was a little bronze thing the size of a palm: a round pot-belly, three feet below, two ears standing up from the rim, a skin of green rust with a dull gold showing through it — like the incense burner on the village shrine's altar, squeezed down a hundredfold. A lid sat on its mouth, and on the lid crouched a little beast, which yawned, opened one eye to glance at him, and shut it again. Silver Moon's voice was very soft: "From my belly. Swallowed it who knows what year… it eats qi; it's been eating mine for years… Look after it for me. It eats anything… feed it, and it spits something out… what it spits, that's your luck… nine times in ten, junk… feed it common things, and mostly common things come out; for an immortal grade, feed it immortal grade… every time it opens, it takes a bite of you…" The voice grew smaller and smaller. Xiaoman called, "Silver Moon?"

She didn't finish. Her body faded like the last wisp of smoke in a stove, faded till even the outline was nearly gone. All that was left was half a sentence, very, very soft:

"…Next time… hit back…"

Xiaoman clutched the token in his palm and called "Silver Moon" twice; no answer. The curled little fox was still there, but of its nine tails the one that had glowed was dark. He stared at it till his palm was all sweat, and then saw that tail, very, very slowly, light once, and go dark again.

Still there.

Only then did he let out a long breath — too hard; his ribs bent him double. Next time, hit back. She wasn't telling him to hit back today. She meant: today, this is how it is; next time, hit back. He put those words away in his heart.

Tonight was the first night of the half-month Ma Xiaobao had promised.

He pulled himself up by the woodpile; his ribs went *crack* and he fell to his knees again. Broken, at least one. He dug the night-watch token out from the bottom of the woodpile and hung it back on his belt, and tucked Little Zheng and the little bronze furnace into his coat. The wall was beyond him; at its foot there was a drain gap, and he lay down and crawled out through it inch by inch, onto the path up the back mountain. Every zhang of path he rested three times, and resting he didn't dare breathe deep, only through that opening neither deep nor shallow, breath by breath. The moon had moved from one side of the sky to the other by the time he reached the garden gate. He lifted the watch book hanging by it; his hand, mud or blood, he couldn't tell, pressed into the box for the twelfth night, and left a print, black and red.

And so he sat, his back against the garden gate, till dawn.

Towards dawn there were footsteps on the path, a step and a stop. It was Sun Ergou, a cloth soaked in well water in his hand. Sun Ergou's bunk was by the little window of the long room, and the patch behind the woodshed could be seen plain from that window. He squatted and pressed the cloth on Xiaoman's swollen left eye, and after a long while said quietly, "…I didn't come out." Xiaoman said, "I know." Sun Ergou said, "I was scared." Xiaoman said, "So was I. Being scared's no shame." Sun Ergou hung his head, and his ears slowly went red. "When I… can stand steady." The second half he didn't say.

On the thirteenth of the tenth month, propped up by Sun Ergou, Xiaoman went to the refectory. Not going, he thought, would look more like something had happened. The whole room stole glances at him, then stole glances at Ma Xiaobao. Everyone knew what had happened. No one said it. Ma Xiaobao, carrying his empty bowl past Xiaoman's table, poked a finger into his shoulder — right on the spot of the twenty-third. "Brother, that was a nasty fall. You lie down and rest; the herb garden, your senior will see to it."

Ah He had come down from the hill — at the hour of mao she had gone into the herb garden and seen the box for the twelfth night in the watch book. She sat down opposite with her bowl and looked at his face first, from left eye to the corner of his mouth. "Who?" Xiaoman said, "I fell." Ah He made a note in her book, her hand shielding it; he saw a circle anyway. Ah He said, "The mud prints on your clothes. One print, one blow. I counted. Twenty-three." Xiaoman started. From under her bowl she took a boiled egg, still warm, and put it in front of him. "Eat it." Xiaoman said, "…On account?" Ah He took up her charcoal and set it to the paper and stopped a long time; the point pressed a little black dot that slowly spread into a ring. Then she made her note and shut the book. "Interest, this time… not counted." She picked up her bowl and left, and not once did she look back.

Outside the refectory, at the dispensary door, stood the Jishi Hall's porters with a delivery of herbs, and behind the loads a barefoot errand boy. Xiaoman knew him: the one on the veranda who'd shouted "Then I'll be that one." The boy took a letter from his coat, addressed in his uncle's hand: To be opened by my nephew Shen Xiaoman.

The letter was short. All well at home, don't worry. Your mother's eyes are a little worn from sewing at night, nothing serious. The night we buried Shidan, it was this boy who helped me dig the grave. The last line was written smaller: **Your father goes into the Heisong Ridge every day now. The Ma dogs won't pass the broken stele; he does. His knee is worse than last year — on overcast days he can't get off the kang, and on clear days he goes anyway. I can't talk him out of it.**

Xiaoman read the letter three times, then tucked it into his coat against the token.

In the hour of Chen that morning Xiaoman didn't go to the lecture. He squatted in the woodshed with the little bronze furnace in front of him and talked to it: "What's your name?" The lid didn't move.

snub.zh: 炉盖纹丝不动。小兽睁开一只眼睛，瞥了你一眼，又闭上了。
snub.en: The lid doesn't stir. The little beast opens one eye, glances at you, and shuts it again.

exits.means: names the furnace 九转金丹炉 — the lid ignores it

snub.zh: 仍是不动。小兽翻了个身，拿屁股对着你。
snub.en: Still nothing. The little beast rolls over and turns its backside to you.

label.en: One Furnace of Heaven and Earth

exits.means: names the furnace 乾坤一炉 — the lid ignores it

snub.zh: 炉盖纹丝不动。小兽打了个大大的哈欠，连眼皮都懒得抬。
snub.en: The lid doesn't stir. The little beast gives a huge yawn, too lazy even to lift an eyelid.

exits.means: names the furnace 饭桶 (rice bucket) — the only name it takes; takes the furnace, keeps it

story.zh:
他一口气报了七八个镇上说书先生嘴里的名号，「镇天神炉」「九转金丹炉」「乾坤一炉」，越报越长，越报越响，它连动都懒得动。他从昨儿夜里到这会儿，只喝了一碗粥、吃了一个鸡蛋，肚子咕咕地叫，终于骂了一声：「你这饭桶，倒比我还难伺候。」只听「咔哒」一声，炉盖轻轻一跳，那小兽睁开一只眼睛，冲他眨了一眨——它看上的，偏偏是「饭桶」两个字。

它肚子上刻着一圈画，细得要眯起眼睛看：山，水，一条弯弯的河，河边一座方方的城。他拿拇指一拃，拃不满它半圈。可昨夜揣了一路，今早再托起来，他总觉得它比昨夜沉了一点。
story.en:
He reeled off seven or eight names out of the town storyteller's mouth — "Heaven-Quelling Divine Furnace", "Nine-Turn Golden Elixir Furnace", "One Furnace of Heaven and Earth" — each longer and grander than the last, and it couldn't be bothered to stir. Since last night he'd had one bowl of gruel and one egg; his stomach growled, and at last he swore: "You rice bucket — you're harder to please than I am." *Click* — the lid gave a little jump, and the little beast opened one eye and blinked at him. The one name it fancied, of all things, was "rice bucket".

All round its belly ran a band of pictures, so fine he had to squint: mountains, water, a winding river, and by the river a square-walled town. He set his thumb and spread his hand; one span didn't reach halfway round. Yet he'd carried it all night, and lifting it again this morning, he couldn't shake the feeling it weighed a little more than it had last night.

refuse.zh: 炉盖纹丝不动。炉盖上的小兽打了个哈欠。
refuse.en: The lid doesn't stir. The little beast on the lid yawns.
